Soluble complex of the mitochondrial intermembrane space composed of various combinations of small Tim proteins; acts as a protein transporter to guide proteins to the Tim22 complex for insertion into the mitochondrial inner membrane.

 TIM22 mitochondrial import inner membrane insertion complex (GO:0042721)
A multi-subunit complex embedded in the mitochondrial inner membrane that mediates the inner membrane insertion of multi-transmembrane spanning proteins that contain internal targeting elements. In yeast cells, TIM22 is a 300-kDa complex, consisting of four membrane integral subunits, Tim22, Tim54, Tim18 and Sdh3, and a peripheral chaperone complex consisting of the small TIM proteins, Tim9-Tim10-Tim12. [PMID:27554484, PMID:12191765]

author: hattrill
body:
Yes, I can kind of see why insertases are a classes as protein carrier chaperone - mechanisically, they are quite strange - they mediate the partition of the hydrophobic portion of the TM protein into the bilayer by providing hydrophobic interaction interfaces. However, it becomes blurred with TM transport as a TIM23 variant TIM23SORT acts as an insertase rather than a TM transporter...

For Tim9 and Tim10, GO:0140318 protein transporter activity is just as valid as protein carrier chaperone when comparing the MF defs. As they are intergral to transport, perhaps protein transporter activity  is ok (just not TM transporter activity)

author: ValWood
body: Most publications depict and describe tim10/12 as actual chaperones: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S002228361200784X They are in the intermembrane space and bind to the cargo. But I don't think it is correct to describe as transporters (even though they are involved in the transport process), because the movement is 'not directed' which is necessary to describe a a transporter. That's why "protein carrier chaperone" isn't a transporter. The thing I find odd is describing an integrate as a "protein carrier chaperone", but maybe that is OK?

author: hattrill
body: I also find the integrase odd as a chaperone - I think with both integrases and the tim9-10 there are arguments to have them as transporters and/or chaperones.

author: hattrill
body:
My broad concern is that is no real way to tell between 'protein transporter activity' and 'protein carrier chaperone':

**protein transporter activity**
Directly binding to a specific protein and delivering it to a specific cellular location. PMID:18706423 
synonyms:
protein transport chaperone 	related
protein carrier activity 	related

**protein carrier chaperone**
Binding to and carrying a protein between two different cellular components by moving along with the target protein. PMID:7628437 
protein carrier activity 	exact
protein chaperone 	broad

I agree that there are 'chaperones' involved in TM transport, but it would be difficult choose the correct term and their MFs are not all equivalent. I would like a consistent way to group/describe these activities as they are very much coupled to TM transport/membrane protein insertion but I do not think we have the correct terms to describe them. I also wonder whether GO:0051082 unfolded protein binding is often used instead of something more satisfactory. I have divided the examples I have come across into three broad classes, but there may be more:

1. **Holdases**:
e.g. Tim8-Tim13 - soluble, mitochondrial intermembrane space chaperone. Tim8-Tim3 complex mediates the import of a small subset of proteins 
and Tim9-Tim10 Is described as a peripheral membrane protein of the TIM22 complex (GO:0042721) or soluble, mitochondrial intermembrane space chaperone
They act to bind unfolded proteins as they emerge from the TOMM complex and keep them in a translocation-competent conformation in the mitochondrial intermembrane space to present them to the SAM or TIM22 complex.

('holdase activity' is general chaperone activity https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.mie.2024.07.051 )


2. **ATPase rachets/motors**:
2a. mitochondrial HSP70/HSPA9: The majority of mtHSP70/HSPA9 acts as a protein folding chaperone in the mitochondrial matrix. A small proportion is part of the presequence translocase-associated motor (PAM) is a subcomplex of the TIM23 complex. In this, mtHSP70/HSPA9 binds precursor proteins to promote their unidirectional translocation across the two mitochondrial membranes and into the mitochondrial matrix by pulling them through the TIM23 complex pore. This is achieved by cycles of high-low affinity binding driven by ATP hydrolysis that generates a pulling force. 
2b. ER HSP70/BiP: Which assists nascent peptide transit through the Sec61 translocon into the ER. This is slightly different to the mechanism of HSP70/HSPA9, ER HSP70/BiP does not generate pulling forces but stabilizes nascent chains by preventing backsliding through ATP-driven cycles of binding and release. PMID:34360841

(note: looks like annotations to GO:0015450 protein-transporting ATPase activity could do with a review)

3. **Unfoldases**:
e.g. PEX1/PEX6 (Peroxisomal membrane extraction complex). An ATPase chaperone complex that interacts with monoubiquitinated Pex5 cargo receptor in the peroxisomal retrotranslocon complex. Mediates ATP-dependent unfolding of Pex5 and extracts it into the cytosol. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02474-4

(note protein unfoldase activity is a broad synonym for GO:0140545 ATP-dependent protein disaggregase activity, but is this activity not also a type of chaperone?)

It is also unclear to me why some activities* are classed as transport and others as chaperone:

```
protein transporter activity GO:0140318
	|_membrane protein dislocase activity GO:0140567 (ATP-dep extraction)*
	|_protein transmembrane transporter activity GO:0008320
	|_lipoprotein releasing activity GO:0140306 (ATP-dependent extrusion)*

protein carrier chaperone GO:0140597
	|_lipoprotein carrier activity GO:0140598*
	|_histone chaperone activity GO:0140713
	|_membrane insertase activity GO:0032977*
```

Just also note this here, so it doesn't get lost:
GO:0061742 chaperone-mediated autophagy translocation complex is capable_of protein carrier chaperone - incorrect as this has been used to annotate LAMP2A.  LAMP2A is not a chaperone, chaperones work upstream of LAMP2A which forms a channel/translocon. So, should be capable_of protein transmembrane transport GO:0071806 PMC10549195

So, in summary, I think we need some new terms and a bit of a review of these 2 branches. I can suggest some more specific terms, but I would like to see if there is some broad agreement on this before that.

author: ValWood
body:
I think entities should only be classed as transporters if they transport. 

GO uses a strict definition of transport- transport in its strictest sense, typically implies a directed process, where substances are moved purposefully from one location to another. This is distinct from diffusion, which is random and undirected.

Instead, ATP in chaperones supports protein folding, stabilization, and conformational changes, which can indirectly facilitate "transport-like" processes within the cell.

So  if I understand correctly "carrier chaperones" that protect and support proteins during the transport process,  should not be classed as transporters. 

I'm happy  to be corrected  but it might be simpler and easier to classify  to continue with the stricter definition so as not to blur the boundary between transport and localization. (as an aside: Localization is rarely required in annotation, there are better ways to capture, as part of the actual process in GO-CAM)

author: raymond91125
body:
The definition of GO:0140309 unfolded protein carrier activity is "A protein carrier activity that binds to a protein in an unfolded state and escorts it between two different cellular components." When a holdase functions in a way that does not specify TWO different cellular components, is it still a carrier? 

A more general definition for a holdase MF could be: Binding to unfolded or partially folded proteins to prevent aggregation and maintain soluble, folding-competent state.

author: ValWood
hattrill
body: @ValWood Yes, holdase just keeps something unfolded so it doesn't aggregate. I think that to another cellular component infers cell compartments, in many cases holdases function within a compartment. I will have a good think about it for Monday.

author: hattrill
body: Hi @srengel just following up on the initial point of the ticket. In the end the decision was to create **'unfolded protein holdase activity' GO:0140309**. This should be used to replace 'protein transporter activity' for the small Tims (TIM9, TIM10, TIM13, TIM8, TIM12).
